intro: Eight questions about your current job. Your answers stay in your browser: nothing is sent or saved.

questions.dimension: How you feel day to day
questions.text: Most weeks, how do you feel about going to work?

options.label: I mostly look forward to it
It's fine; some good days, some bad

questions.text: How often does work stress follow you home, into your evenings, weekends or sleep?

options.label: Most of the time, and it's affecting my sleep or health

questions.text: Compared with similar roles, do you think you're paid fairly?

options.label: Yes, at or above what similar roles pay

questions.text: Are you still learning and moving forward in this job?

options.label: No, and there's no path to change that here

questions.text: How do you get on with your manager and the people you work with?
How well do the hours, commute and flexibility fit the rest of your life?
How secure does your job feel over the next year?

options.label: I expect to lose it, or it's ending

questions.text: If you started looking, how much time could you give it each week?

stay.title: It sounds like a good place to be, for now.
stay.body: Nothing in your answers is pushing you out. Keep your CV up to date and your LinkedIn current, so that if something changes, or a great role appears, you're ready without starting from scratch.

fix_first.title: It might be worth trying to fix one thing first.
fix_first.body: Most of your job works for you, but one area doesn't. Problems like this can sometimes be solved where you are, which is faster and less tiring than a search. If raising it doesn't change anything within a few months, that's a clear signal to start looking.

explore.title: It's worth exploring quietly.
explore.body: A few things aren't right, but nothing is urgent. A light search lets you see what's out there without pressure: update your CV, track a few applications to roles that would genuinely be better, and see what comes back.

move.title: Your answers suggest it's time to look.
move.body: Several important things aren't working. That's a good reason to plan a proper search, one you can keep up for a few months, rather than a burst of applications on a bad day.

fix_tips.stress: Talk to your manager about workload: name the two or three things taking most of your time and ask what can move. If your employer has an Employee Assistance Programme, it's confidential and free to use.
fix_tips.pay: Gather salary ranges from job ads for similar roles in your area, then ask for a pay review with those figures. A specific, evidenced request is easier to say yes to.
fix_tips.growth: Ask your manager what a next step would look like here and what you'd need to show. If there's no answer, that's useful information too.
fix_tips.people: If it's one relationship, a direct, calm conversation sometimes helps; if it's more serious, HR or a trusted senior colleague can be the next step.
fix_tips.life_fit: Ask whether hours, hybrid days or start times can change. Many employers have more flexibility than they advertise.

wellbeing_note: If work stress is affecting your sleep or health, look after that first: it matters more than any job search. Your GP is a good place to start, and so is your employer's Employee Assistance Programme if there is one.
pay_unsure_note: Not sure what fair pay looks like? Compare salary ranges in job ads for similar roles in your area. Hearback shows salary ranges on matched jobs where employers publish them.

expectations.funnel: Out of 100 people who apply for a typical role, about 8 get a first call, about 3 reach the final interviews and about 1 gets the offer. Silence is the usual outcome, not a verdict on you.
expectations.source: Gem conversion benchmarks (about 12 million candidates, mostly US).
expectations.pace: Plan a pace you could keep up for a few months, rather than a burst of applications on a bad day.
expectations.hours_per_application_note: Assumes about 1.5 hours to find, tailor and send one good application. Adjust to your own pace.
while_employed: Use your own phone, laptop and email for your search, never your work ones.
On LinkedIn, 'Open to work' can be set to recruiters only.
Check your notice period in your contract before you accept anything.
Book interviews early or late in the day, or take leave; you don't owe anyone an explanation.

in_a_year.question: Would this still bother you in a year?

labels.lasts: People rarely get used to this. A solid reason.
labels.fades: Feels big now, but the lift from fixing it tends to fade.

in_a_year.glow_note: New jobs usually feel great for the first few months, then settle. Studies of people who change jobs find satisfaction jumps after a move and drifts back over the following year. That's not a reason to stay. It's a reason to move towards something specific, not just away from a bad week.
in_a_year.fades_only_note: Your main reason is one that tends to fade. A pay rise, a bigger title or a fresh start feels great at first, then becomes normal. Before you move for this alone, check that the new job would also be better on something that lasts: your manager and team, your commute and hours, how much you're learning.

sources.label: Boswell, Boudreau & Tichy (2005), The relationship between employee job change and job satisfaction: the honeymoon-hangover effect, Journal of Applied Psychology 90(5)
Stutzer & Frey (2008), Stress that doesn't pay: the commuting paradox, Scandinavian Journal of Economics 110(2)
